shortDef: The controls that let people move between parts of a product.
longDef: Navigation has to answer three questions at once: where am I, where can I go, and how do I get back. Its labels are the most-read text in any product, which makes wording more important than styling. Structure comes first — no navigation design rescues a bad information architecture.
example: A tab bar marking the current section, plus a back affordance on every pushed screen, answers all three questions.

shortDef: A trail showing where a page sits in the hierarchy.
longDef: Breadcrumbs show the path from the top level to the current page and let people jump up a level in one tap. They are most valuable on deep, hierarchical sites and on pages people arrive at from search, with no sense of context. They supplement navigation rather than replacing it.
example: Home › Support › Deliveries › Missing parcel, where every step before the last is tappable.
misuse: A breadcrumb showing the path the user took, rather than the site hierarchy, is a history trail and confuses more than it helps.

shortDef: A persistent row of top-level destinations, usually along the bottom.
longDef: Tab bars keep three to five destinations permanently visible and one tap away, which makes the product's shape obvious. They work when the sections are peers and mutually exclusive. Beyond five items labels stop fitting and the bar becomes a row of guesses.
example: Search, Browse, Revise and Saved, each with an icon and a label, with the current tab marked by more than colour.
misuse: Tabs are for switching between places, not for actions. A tab that opens a modal breaks the model.

shortDef: Navigation hidden behind a three-line icon.
longDef: The pattern trades discoverability for screen space: everything is available but nothing is visible. Measured against visible navigation it consistently reduces engagement with the sections inside it. It remains reasonable for genuinely secondary destinations, and unreasonable for the main ones.
example: Moving "Saved" out of a drawer and into a visible tab typically increases its use several times over.
misuse: Adding the word "Menu" beside the icon helps recognition but does not fix the underlying cost of hiding things.

shortDef: A window that blocks the rest of the interface until dismissed.
longDef: Modality forces a single decision by making everything else unavailable, which is why it suits confirmation of destructive actions and little else. It costs the user their context and, on small screens, most of the display. Focus must move into it and return to where it came from on close.
example: "Delete this project and its 12 files? This cannot be undone", with Cancel and Delete, and nothing else reachable.
misuse: Using a modal for content people need to refer back to forces them to memorise it. Use a page or a sheet instead.

shortDef: A panel that slides up from the bottom edge, over the content.
longDef: Sheets put options within thumb reach and keep the underlying context partly visible, which makes them a gentler alternative to a full modal on phones. They can be non-modal, letting the page behind stay live. Anything taller than half the screen should probably be a page.
example: Tapping share raises a sheet of destinations without leaving the article behind it.

shortDef: A brief message confirming something happened.
longDef: A toast appears without taking focus, states an outcome and disappears. It suits confirmations and low-stakes information, sometimes with a single action such as undo. Anything the user must act on, or must be able to re-read, belongs somewhere persistent — a toast is gone in seconds and invisible to a screen reader unless announced.
example: "Saved." appearing above the tab bar after a save, paired with a live-region announcement.
misuse: Errors in a toast are a common failure. If the user has to fix something, the message must stay on screen.

shortDef: A small label revealed on hover or focus explaining a control.
longDef: Tooltips supplement a control that is already understandable, adding detail for those who want it. They fail on touch, where there is no hover, and they hide information behind an interaction that many users never perform. Anything essential should be visible instead.
example: Hovering a chart legend reveals the exact definition of the metric, which is also stated in the report below.
misuse: A tooltip is not a fix for an unlabelled icon. If the icon needs explaining, it needs a label.

shortDef: Stacked sections that expand one at a time to reveal content.
longDef: Accordions compress a long page into scannable headings, letting people open only what they need. They work when the headings are genuinely self-describing and the sections are independent. They hurt when users need to compare sections, or when the content inside is what everyone came for.
example: A product page collapsing delivery, returns and materials into three headings, with none open by default.
misuse: Collapsing content people always read adds a tap for everyone. Measure before hiding.

shortDef: A rotating set of panels shown one or a few at a time.
longDef: Carousels promise several messages in one slot and usually deliver one: engagement drops sharply after the first panel. They work better as manually scrolled lists of peers — related products, photos — than as auto-rotating hero banners. Auto-advance is a particular problem for anyone who reads slowly or relies on a screen reader.
example: A horizontally scrolling row of related items, with the next one partly visible, and no automatic movement.
misuse: Auto-rotating banners are the canonical example: they move away mid-read and are widely ignored as adverts.

shortDef: New content loads automatically as the user reaches the bottom.
longDef: It suits open-ended browsing where there is no destination, and it makes returning to a specific item hard, because position is lost. It also makes the page footer unreachable. A load-more button gives most of the benefit while keeping control and a stable end.
example: A photo feed is a reasonable fit; a search results page where people compare options is not.
misuse: Infinite scroll plus a footer containing important links is a well-known trap — the footer can never be reached.

shortDef: Splitting a long list into numbered pages.
longDef: Pagination gives a sense of how much there is, makes positions stable enough to return to, and keeps each request small. It costs an interaction per page and interrupts browsing. It suits result sets people work through deliberately rather than feeds they graze.
example: Search results showing "page 2 of 14" so the user can judge whether to refine the query instead of scrolling.

shortDef: Grey placeholders in the shape of content that is loading.
longDef: Showing the layout before the data arrives makes a wait feel shorter than a spinner does, because progress appears to be happening and the page does not jump when content lands. It only helps for short waits; beyond a few seconds people need a real progress signal. The skeleton must match the real layout or the shift is worse.
example: Three grey bars where the article title and two lines of summary will appear, replaced in place when loaded.
misuse: A skeleton that never resolves is worse than a spinner, because it looks like content that failed to render.

shortDef: A signal that the system is working, and how far along it is.
longDef: Determinate indicators show proportion completed and suit anything over a few seconds; indeterminate spinners only say that something is happening. Below about a second, showing nothing is better than a flash of loading. Over about ten, say what is happening and roughly how long it will take.
example: "Uploading 3 of 12 files" tells the user more than a spinning circle, and lets them decide whether to wait.
misuse: A spinner with no timeout is the most common way an interface silently fails. Every wait needs an end state.

shortDef: What a screen shows when there is nothing to show.
longDef: Empty states are the first thing new users see and the last thing designed. A good one explains why the space is empty, what will fill it, and offers the action that starts. There are several kinds — first use, no results, everything cleared — and they need different words.
example: "Nothing saved yet. Save a term from its page and it lands here." with a button to find one.
misuse: An illustration with no action is decoration. The empty state's job is to move the person forward.

shortDef: What the interface shows when something has gone wrong.
longDef: A usable error says what happened, why, and what to do next, in the user's language and next to the thing that caused it. It should never blame the user or expose an internal code alone. Recoverable errors keep the user's input intact — losing a filled form to a validation error is its own failure.
example: "That card expired in 2024. Check the expiry date or use another card", shown beside the field, with the number preserved.
misuse: "An error occurred" tells the user nothing they did not already know and offers no way forward.

shortDef: Structuring input so people can complete it without errors.
longDef: The reliable rules are few: one column, labels above fields, related fields grouped, only the questions you genuinely need, and input types that match the data. Every removed field measurably improves completion. Most form problems are content problems — people cannot tell what is being asked.
example: Splitting a 22-field application into four grouped steps with a progress marker raises completion substantially.
misuse: Placeholder text as a label disappears on typing and fails accessibility. Labels stay visible.

shortDef: Checking input and telling the user about problems.
longDef: Validate on blur rather than on every keystroke, so people are not told they are wrong while still typing. Confirm success quietly and describe failure specifically, next to the field. Server-side checks still have to run — client-side validation is a convenience, never the guarantee.
example: Leaving the email field with "name@" shows "That address is missing everything after the @" beneath it.
misuse: Validating as the user types marks a half-entered value as an error, which reads as the interface arguing with you.

shortDef: Formatting a field's value as the user types it.
longDef: Masks add separators to card numbers, dates or phone numbers so the value stays readable and checkable. They must not reject characters the user reasonably types — a pasted number with spaces should be accepted and reformatted. Masks that move the cursor unpredictably are worse than no mask.
example: Typing 4242424242424242 displays as 4242 4242 4242 4242, and pasting the spaced version works identically.
misuse: Blocking input that does not match the mask is a common failure for international phone numbers and postcodes.

shortDef: Suggesting completions as someone types into a field.
longDef: Autocomplete converts recall into recognition, cuts typing and reduces spelling errors — especially valuable on phones. Suggestions must be ranked usefully, keyboard navigable and announced to assistive technology. Autofill from stored data is a related and even higher-value case.
example: Typing "lond" into a destination field offers London Heathrow and London City, with the airport codes shown.
misuse: Suggestions that replace what the user typed on blur cause silent wrong entries. Never overwrite without a deliberate selection.

shortDef: A control that hides a list of options until opened.
longDef: Dropdowns save space at the cost of hiding the options, which makes them poor for short lists and for anything people need to compare. Under about six options, radio buttons or segmented controls are faster and clearer. Above about twenty, add search rather than scrolling.
example: Two options — monthly or yearly — belong as visible radio buttons, not behind a select.
misuse: Using a dropdown for a two-item choice adds two interactions to a decision that could have taken none.

shortDef: Radio buttons, checkboxes and switches, each with a distinct meaning.
longDef: Radio buttons choose one from several and cannot be unset once chosen; checkboxes allow any number including none; switches turn one setting on or off and take effect immediately. Using the wrong one misleads people about what will happen. A switch implies instant effect, so a switch inside a form with a Save button is a contradiction.
example: Delivery speed is radio buttons, marketing preferences are checkboxes, and dark mode is a switch.
misuse: Checkboxes used for a single either-or choice hide the alternative, since an unticked box does not state what happens instead.

shortDef: A calendar control for choosing dates.
longDef: Pickers help when the day of the week or availability matters, and hinder when the date is simply known — a birth date is faster typed than found in a calendar twelve taps back. The strongest pattern offers both: a typed field that accepts several formats, with a calendar available. Ranges need the two ends to remain visible and editable.
example: A hotel booking shows a calendar with unavailable nights disabled; a passport form offers three simple fields instead.
misuse: Forcing a calendar for distant dates is the classic version of this mistake, most visibly on date-of-birth fields.

shortDef: Letting people find content by typing what they want.
longDef: Search is how people who know what they want bypass your structure, and how people whose vocabulary differs from yours get anywhere at all. It needs synonym handling, tolerance for typos and a useful no-results state. Logging queries that return nothing is the cheapest content research available.
example: A dictionary that matches aliases as well as headwords finds "split test" when the entry is filed under "A/B test".
misuse: Zero-result pages that only say "no results" waste the most informative moment in the whole product.

shortDef: Narrowing a set of results by attribute.
longDef: Filters remove items that do not match, and work best when the applied filters stay visible, the result count updates immediately, and combinations that would return nothing are disabled or flagged. They depend entirely on the quality of the underlying metadata. Sorting reorders the same set and should never be confused with filtering.
example: Applying "in stock" and "under £50" shows both as removable chips above a live count of matching items.
misuse: Filters and sorting are often merged into one menu, which leaves people unsure whether items disappeared or moved.

shortDef: Letting people reverse an action instead of confirming it first.
longDef: Undo turns a decision into something recoverable, which lets the interface stop interrupting with confirmations. It is faster for the common case and safer for the mistaken one. It needs a clear window, a visible offer, and genuine reversal — not a message claiming reversal that only hides the change.
example: Deleting an email removes it immediately and offers "Undo" for a few seconds, rather than asking "are you sure?" every time.
misuse: Undo cannot cover everything. Truly irreversible actions — sending money, publishing — still need confirmation.

shortDef: Moving something by picking it up and releasing it elsewhere.
longDef: Direct manipulation is intuitive for reordering and for spatial arrangement, and it demands clear signals: what can be dragged, where it can go, and what happened. It is hard for people with motor impairments and impossible with a screen reader unless a keyboard equivalent exists. Always provide one.
example: A reorderable list where items can also be moved with a "move up" control and with keyboard arrows when focused.
misuse: Drag as the only way to perform an action is an accessibility failure, and one that WCAG 2.2 addresses directly.

shortDef: An action performed by moving a finger on a touchscreen.
longDef: Swipes, pinches and long presses are fast for people who know them and invisible to everyone else, because they leave no trace on screen. Treat them as accelerators layered on top of a visible control, never as the only route. Every gesture also needs an accessible equivalent.
example: Swiping a row to delete, with the same delete available in the row's menu and as a screen-reader action.
misuse: Hidden gestures are a frequent cause of undiscoverable features. If it is not signalled, most people never find it.

shortDef: Dragging a list downward to reload its contents.
longDef: The gesture became a convention because it maps neatly onto the idea of pulling new content into view, and because it needs no permanent control. It is undiscoverable on its own and unavailable to keyboard and switch users. Products that rely on it should also refresh automatically and offer a visible control.
example: A feed that refreshes on pull, refreshes on returning to the screen, and has a refresh item in its menu.

shortDef: The area that responds to a tap, which is larger than the icon.
longDef: Platform guidance puts the minimum at around 44 by 44 points on iOS and 48 by 48 density-independent pixels on Android, and WCAG 2.2 sets 24 by 24 CSS pixels as an absolute floor for the web. The visible mark can be smaller than the target — padding and hit slop extend the area without adding visual weight. Adjacent targets also need space between them.
example: A 16px close icon inside a 44pt tappable area, with 8pt of clearance from the control beside it.
misuse: Sizing the target to the icon is one of the most common mobile defects, and it disproportionately affects people with tremor.

shortDef: The part of a phone screen a thumb reaches comfortably.
longDef: Holding a phone one-handed leaves a natural arc near the bottom and the holding side easy to reach, and the far top corner hard. Frequent and primary actions belong in the easy zone; destructive ones benefit from being harder to hit. Grip varies by hand size and by whether the person is walking, so treat it as a tendency rather than a map.
example: Putting the main action bar at the bottom of a tall screen rather than in a top-right corner nobody can reach.

shortDef: Showing what most people need, with the rest one step away.
longDef: Common options stay visible while advanced ones move behind a clearly labelled control. Done well it reduces load without reducing capability, and the label has to promise what is behind it. Done badly it becomes hidden functionality that only the people who wrote it can find.
example: A share sheet showing three destinations and "More options", rather than twenty at once.
misuse: Hiding something everyone needs is not progressive disclosure, it is an extra tap for the whole audience.

shortDef: Showing the result immediately, before the server confirms it.
longDef: The interface assumes success and updates at once, reconciling later if the request fails. It removes waiting from actions that almost always succeed, such as liking or reordering. It requires a genuine plan for failure — a silent revert leaves the user believing something happened that did not.
example: A bookmark fills in the moment it is tapped; if the write fails, it un-fills with a message explaining why.
misuse: Optimistic updates for actions that often fail, or that involve money, trade trust for a small gain in speed.

shortDef: Pre-selecting the option most people will want.
longDef: Defaults are the most powerful control in an interface, because most people accept them. Setting them from context — country from locale, today's date, the last-used option — removes work without removing choice. The ethical line is that a default must serve the user, not just the business.
example: A delivery form pre-filling the saved address, with a visible option to send it somewhere else.
misuse: A pre-ticked marketing box is a default working against the user, and is unlawful in several jurisdictions.

shortDef: Getting a new user to their first useful outcome.
longDef: The goal is not to explain the product but to get someone to value quickly, ideally by doing something real rather than watching a tour. Explanations work best delivered in context, at the moment they are needed. Onboarding that must be completed before anything can be tried fights the way people actually learn software.
example: A notes app that opens with a new note ready to type, and explains sync the first time a second device appears.
misuse: A carousel of feature screenshots before signup is skipped by most people and remembered by almost none.

shortDef: A small self-contained moment around a single action.
longDef: A microinteraction has a trigger, rules, feedback and a result — a toggle flipping, a field validating, a like animating. They are where a product feels considered or careless, because they are the parts people touch most often. The feedback is the point; the animation is only one way to deliver it.
example: Pulling to refresh: the trigger is the drag, the feedback is the tension and release, the result is fresh content.
misuse: Not a synonym for animation. A microinteraction with no animation at all can still be well designed.

shortDef: Physical feedback delivered through vibration.
longDef: A short tap confirms an action without requiring the user to look, which is valuable when the device is in a pocket, when someone is walking, or when vision is limited. It has to be sparing and meaningful — constant buzzing is quickly turned off. Platforms define standard intensities for selection, success and warning.
example: A light tap when a flashcard flips, and a slightly heavier one when an answer is graded.
misuse: Haptics as the only signal excludes people who have them disabled, and anyone using a device without them.

shortDef: A bounded container grouping one item's content and actions.
longDef: Cards make a set of things scannable by drawing a region around each, and they rearrange easily across screen sizes. They cost vertical space and, used everywhere, flatten hierarchy into a uniform grid where nothing leads. A list row is often the better answer when scanning matters more than presence.
example: A term-of-the-day card with a heading, a one-line definition and a category, tappable as a single unit.
misuse: Nested cards inside cards remove the grouping signal entirely, because everything is inside a boundary.

shortDef: A visual hint that there is more content below or beside.
longDef: People scroll readily, but only when something tells them there is more. Content cut off at the fold, a partially visible next card, or a fading edge all signal continuation. A section that ends exactly at the viewport edge reads as the end of the page.
example: A horizontal row that shows half of the next item, so the row obviously continues past the screen edge.

shortDef: The small pieces of text that guide people through an interface.
longDef: Button labels, hints, error text, empty states and confirmations do more usability work per word than anything else in a product. Buttons should name their outcome rather than say "submit", and hints should answer the question the field provokes. Small wording changes routinely move completion rates more than layout changes do.
example: Changing a button from "Submit" to "Save term", with the confirmation reading "Saved."
misuse: Microcopy is not decoration or personality. Jokes in an error message make a bad moment worse.

shortDef: Writing so people understand it the first time they read it.
longDef: Plain language means short sentences, common words, active voice and the important thing first. It is not dumbing down: experts read plain writing faster too, and under stress everyone's reading ability drops. Legal and technical accuracy can almost always survive the rewrite.
example: "We will refund you within five working days" instead of "reimbursement shall be effected within the stated period".

shortDef: The consistent personality of a product, adjusted to context.
longDef: Voice is constant — the character the product always has. Tone shifts with the situation: the same product is warm in a welcome and plain in a payment failure. Documenting both, with examples of what each sounds like in an error, is what keeps a large team consistent.
example: A playful voice still writes "Your payment did not go through" rather than attempting a joke at that moment.
misuse: Applying one tone everywhere is the common failure. Cheerfulness during a failure reads as indifference.

shortDef: An interface designed to trick people into acting against their interests.
longDef: Deceptive patterns include hiding the cancel path, pre-ticked consent, fake scarcity, confirmshaming and making the unsubscribe route deliberately long. They convert measurably in the short term and are increasingly illegal, most explicitly under EU and UK consumer rules. The reliable test is whether you would explain the design to the user honestly.
example: A subscription that takes one tap to start and a phone call during business hours to cancel.
misuse: Not every persuasive design is deceptive. The line is whether the user's understanding is being deliberately impaired.

shortDef: A common solution that reliably makes things worse.
longDef: An anti-pattern is a recurring response to a problem that seems reasonable and produces predictable damage — mystery-meat icons, modal onboarding tours, infinite scroll on search results. Naming them helps teams reject them without re-litigating the reasoning each time. Unlike deceptive patterns, they are usually well intentioned.
example: Replacing labelled navigation with icons alone saves space and reliably reduces the use of every section.
misuse: An anti-pattern is not always wrong. It is wrong often enough that using one needs a reason.

shortDef: A shared expectation about how something works.
longDef: Conventions are learned from the wider ecosystem: a logo returns home, a magnifying glass means search, a red badge means unread. They are not laws, but breaking one spends attention that could have gone on your actual product. Conventions also differ by platform, which is why an iOS pattern transplanted to Android often feels wrong.
example: Placing the primary action on the right on iOS and following the platform's own ordering on Android.

shortDef: How things are normally done on a specific operating system.
longDef: iOS and Android differ in navigation, back behaviour, typography, sheet behaviour and system gestures, and users of each have expectations built by every other app they own. Cross-platform products decide how much to unify and how much to respect each platform. Back behaviour and system gestures are the ones you break at your peril.
example: Android's system back gesture must dismiss a sheet; ignoring it makes the app feel broken rather than distinctive.
